Module 8: Autoregressive Distributed Lag Models

Econ 6376 — Applied Time Series Econometrics

How to Use These Notes

This chapter has one main reading path and three optional layers.

  • Core material is the main text. It contains the concepts, notation, interpretations, and applied skills expected of everyone.
  • Deeper Dive sections explain why a result works or develop it more fully. They are useful, but they can be skipped on a first reading.
  • Technical Note sections state qualifications or formal details that matter for precise reasoning.
  • Looking Ahead sections introduce an idea that will be taught formally in a later module.

If you missed lecture, read the main text, run the Core code, and complete the Core Practice problems. Then return to the optional sections that address your questions or interests. The previews of Granger causality and cointegration are orientation for Modules 9–10, not additional assessable material in Module 8.

Core Learning Objectives

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

  1. Translate a time-unrolled diagram into an ARDL equation, distinguishing observed-variable lags, innovation lags, and contemporaneous relationships.
  2. Write and interpret an ARDL(p,q)(p,q), including its restricted cases, and distinguish it from a regression with ARMA disturbances.
  3. Explain the condition E[ϵt∣ℱt−1,xt]=0E[\epsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0, why it involves the whole regressor information set, and how common current shocks differ from lagged feedback.
  4. Use simulation to distinguish sampling variability from failure to recover structural coefficients, and explain why clean residuals do not establish exogeneity or causal identification.
  5. Calculate impact, pulse, cumulative, and stable long-run multipliers. Distinguish an imposed path for xx from a shock to a persistent xx process and from a causal intervention.
  6. Fit a stationary ARDL by OLS under the maintained assumptions, compare modest lag specifications on a common sample, and inspect regression residuals.
  7. Construct a forecast using information available at its origin, identify when future predictor values must themselves be forecast, and explain the uncertainty a conditional forecast leaves out.
  8. Evaluate an ARDL against univariate benchmarks on the same dates and explain the limitations of a forecast exercise using revised historical data.

8.1 Letting a Second Variable into the Room — Core

The Module 7 Handoff

Module 7 compared and combined forecasts made from a series’ own history. Combining forecasts can rearrange the information in that pool; it cannot supply information absent from every member. The next question is therefore concrete: could initial unemployment-insurance claims tell us something about unemployment that unemployment’s own history does not?

The autoregressive distributed lag model, abbreviated ARDL or ADL, gives us a first way to put that question into an equation. It also gives us a first encounter with the complications of multivariate time series: feedback, common shocks, reporting delays, and long-run relationships.

We begin with pictures. A directed acyclic graph (DAG) contains directed arrows and no path that follows those arrows back to its starting node. Here we unroll time: yt−1y_{t-1} and yty_t are different nodes. That lets us depict feedback across dates without drawing a cycle within a date. The diagrams are small fragments of a longer time sequence.

What an ARMA Diagram Contains

For an ARMA(1,1)(1,1),

yt=α+ϕ1yt−1+θ1ϵt−1+ϵt, y_t=\alpha+\phi_1y_{t-1}+\theta_1\epsilon_{t-1}+\epsilon_t,

the outcome remembers past outcomes and past innovations. The following diagram shows those two routes into the current outcome. Deterministic terms are omitted from the picture.

The arrow ϵt−1→yt\epsilon_{t-1}\to y_t corresponds to θ1ϵt−1\theta_1\epsilon_{t-1}. The route ϵt−1→yt−1→yt\epsilon_{t-1}\to y_{t-1}\to y_t also carries part of last period’s innovation forward. These are not competing definitions of memory; they are two routes through the equation.

What Changes in an ARDL Diagram

Now replace the explicit MA term with current and lagged observations of another series:

yt=α+ϕ1yt−1+β0xt+β1xt−1+ϵt. y_t=\alpha+\phi_1y_{t-1}+\beta_0x_t+\beta_1x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t.

The new information is observed xx, not a past innovation. Its coefficient can differ across dates: β0\beta_0 need not equal β1\beta_1. In a monthly labor-market application, employers’ layoffs and unemployed workers’ job finding need not affect the unemployment rate on the same schedule.

Read the arrows carefully. These pictures represent posited dependencies in a model. Drawing xt→ytx_t\to y_t is not evidence that changing xtx_t would cause a change in yty_t. The within-period ordering is an assumption to investigate. We will make that issue central in §8.3.

Pause and predict. Which diagram term could still be present if the current value of xx were unavailable? Which arrow would disappear if the outcome had no own persistence? Write the corresponding restrictions before moving on.

The Mixing Board

The familiar master equation was

yt=α+δt+∑j=1pϕjyt−j+∑ℓ=1qθℓϵt−ℓ+ϵt. y_t=\alpha+\delta t+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_jy_{t-j} +\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\theta_\ell\epsilon_{t-\ell}+\epsilon_t.

We expand the board with a new observed-variable block. The baseline ARDL sets the explicit MA block and deterministic trend to zero:

Slider Earlier univariate models Module 8 baseline
Intercept α\alpha Available On
Deterministic trend δt\delta t Available Off in our stationary examples
Outcome lags ϕjyt−j\phi_j y_{t-j} On in AR/ARMA On
Innovation lags θℓϵt−ℓ\theta_\ell\epsilon_{t-\ell} On in MA/ARMA Off
Predictor block ∑ℓ=0qβℓxt−ℓ\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell x_{t-\ell} Absent New
Current disturbance ϵt\epsilon_t Present Present; its relation to xx now needs attention

This module’s sequence is Concept → Math → Simulate → Real Data: the diagrams and equations establish the model; §8.3 states the assumptions; §8.4 deliberately breaks them; §§8.5–8.7 trace responses and apply the model. The short optional previews at the end do not repeat a full application workflow.

8.2 One Conditional Equation — Core

Start with ARDL(1,1)

In

yt=α+ϕ1yt−1+β0xt+β1xt−1+ϵt, y_t=\alpha+\phi_1y_{t-1}+\beta_0x_t+\beta_1x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t,

ϕ1\phi_1 describes outcome persistence, β0\beta_0 is the contemporaneous xx coefficient, and β1\beta_1 is the direct lagged-xx contribution holding the other regressors fixed. The intercept is α\alpha, not automatically the unconditional mean of yy.

For example, if α=0.2\alpha=0.2, ϕ1=0.6\phi_1=0.6, β0=0.4\beta_0=0.4, and β1=0.2\beta_1=0.2, then yt−1=2y_{t-1}=2, xt=1x_t=1, and xt−1=0.5x_{t-1}=0.5 imply a conditional mean of 0.2+0.6(2)+0.4(1)+0.2(0.5)=1.90.2+0.6(2)+0.4(1)+0.2(0.5)=1.9, provided the remaining disturbance has conditional mean zero. The realization is 1.9+ϵt1.9+\epsilon_t, not necessarily 1.9.

After estimation, we instead write

yt=α̂+ϕ̂1yt−1+β̂0xt+β̂1xt−1+et. y_t=\hat\alpha+\hat\phi_1y_{t-1} +\hat\beta_0x_t+\hat\beta_1x_{t-1}+e_t.

The fitted value ŷt\hat y_t is the estimated right-hand side without ete_t. The residual is et=yt−ŷte_t=y_t-\hat y_t. Hats denote estimates; the true DGP parameters and ϵt\epsilon_t remain unobserved outside a simulation. From Module 7 onward, an actual forecast carries a tilde, ỹt+h∣t\tilde y_{t+h\mid t}.

Generalize Only After the Pieces Are Familiar

An ARDL(p,q)(p,q) with one predictor is

yt=α+∑j=1pϕjyt−j+∑ℓ=0qβℓxt−ℓ+ϵt. y_t=\alpha+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_jy_{t-j} +\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell x_{t-\ell}+\epsilon_t.

Here pp is the maximum outcome lag and qq is the maximum predictor lag. In an ARMA(p,q)(p,q), qq meant the MA order. The model name tells you which meaning applies. Our ARDL convention includes current xx; an application may restrict β0=0\beta_0=0 and use only lagged predictors.

Restriction Result
All βℓ=0\beta_\ell=0 AR(p)(p)
All ϕj=0\phi_j=0 Distributed-lag regression
q=0q=0 Current xx plus outcome lags
β0=0\beta_0=0 ARDL with only lagged xx terms

There can be several predictors, each with its own lag length. We use one so that timing and interpretation remain visible. Adding five series and twenty lags does not remove the need to justify each information set.

ARDL and Regression with ARMA Disturbances

An ARDL is not simply another name for every regression involving dependent observations. Compare

ARDL:yt=α+ϕ1yt−1+β0xt+β1xt−1+ϵt,Regression with AR(1) disturbances:yt=α+βxt+ut,ut=ϕ1ut−1+ϵt. \begin{aligned} \text{ARDL:}\qquad y_t&=\alpha+\phi_1y_{t-1}+\beta_0x_t+\beta_1x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t,\\ \text{Regression with AR(1) disturbances:}\qquad y_t&=\alpha+\beta x_t+u_t,\qquad u_t=\phi_1u_{t-1}+\epsilon_t. \end{aligned}

In the second model, serial dependence is specified for utu_t, the disturbance around the static regression relationship. Substituting its equation gives

yt=(1−ϕ1)α+ϕ1yt−1+βxt−ϕ1βxt−1+ϵt. y_t=(1-\phi_1)\alpha+\phi_1y_{t-1}+\beta x_t-\phi_1\beta x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t.

That is a restricted ARDL: the lagged predictor coefficient must equal −ϕ1β-\phi_1\beta. An unrestricted ARDL estimates the two predictor coefficients separately. More general ARMA disturbances introduce additional structure. Check the software model before translating an xreg coefficient into an ARDL multiplier.

The Stationary Baseline

For the main workflow, we work with stationary variables and a stable dynamic equation. The AR lag polynomial remains

Φ(L)=1−ϕ1L−⋯−ϕpLp.\Phi(L)=1-\phi_1L-\cdots-\phi_pL^p.

All its roots must lie outside the unit circle for stable conditional outcome dynamics. For ARDL(1,1)(1,1) this reduces to |ϕ1|<1|\phi_1|<1. With stationary xx and suitable stationary disturbances, this permits a stationary solution for yy. If xx also responds to past yy, stability of the joint system must be checked; the outcome coefficient alone is not enough.

Do not feed trending levels into a conventional stationary-regression workflow and interpret the usual output automatically. Modules 1–2 showed why unrelated random walks can look related. Cointegration provides an important alternative for some nonstationary series; §8.9 previews it. It is not a blanket permission to regress one wandering series on another.

8.3 Exogeneity: What Is Left in the Disturbance? — Core

Start with the Economic Timing

Suppose monthly inflation is yty_t and the federal funds rate is xtx_t. A positive association could reflect policy responding to inflation, a delayed effect of policy, or both responding to other news. A regression table does not choose among these stories for us.

Calling a column an “independent variable” only identifies where we put it in the regression. It does not establish independence or exogeneity. We need an assumption about what is left out of the equation and how that omitted part relates to the included information.

Let ℱt−1\mathcal F_{t-1} contain the relevant histories of yy and xx through period t−1t-1. A sufficient conditional-mean assumption for our baseline equation is

E[ϵt∣ℱt−1,xt]=0. \boxed{E[\epsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0.}

Read it as: once we account for the history and current xx, the remaining disturbance has mean zero. This is a statement about the whole conditioning information set, not a collection of separate pairwise independence claims. Under it, the ARDL right-hand side without ϵt\epsilon_t really is the specified conditional mean.

For OLS we need valid regressor–disturbance moments. If ztz_t collects the intercept, included yy lags, and included current/lagged xx values, this conditional assumption implies E[ztϵt]=0E[z_t\epsilon_t]=0. Together with appropriate stability, moments, and a nonsingular regressor second-moment matrix, it supports large-sample coefficient consistency. It does not promise exact recovery in a finite sample.

Three Different Relationships

Relationship What it says Does it settle the OLS issue?
xtx_t and yty_t are correlated The variables move together No; we often include xx precisely because they are related.
ϵt\epsilon_t is serially uncorrelated The disturbance does not linearly predict itself across dates No; it can still be correlated with current xtx_t.
E[ϵt∣ℱt−1,xt]=0E[\epsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0 Current regressors and included history do not reveal a remaining conditional-mean component Yes, it supplies the relevant mean restrictions, with other estimation conditions still required.

A disturbance can be white noise and contemporaneously related to another white-noise shock. “No memory” is not “unrelated to every variable in the model.”

Common Current News and Lagged Feedback

We can extend the opening diagram without creating a same-period cycle:

Common current shock. Suppose unexpected layoffs move both initial claims and unemployment within a month. If the outcome disturbance contains part of that news, current claims may be related to the disturbance. A coefficient intended to describe a particular structural effect need not be recovered by OLS. Including the observed predictor can still improve a conditional forecast; prediction and structural interpretation are different questions.

Lagged feedback. Suppose

xt=0.5xt−1+0.2yt−1+ϵx,t.x_t=0.5x_{t-1}+0.2y_{t-1}+\epsilon_{x,t}.

If ϵx,t\epsilon_{x,t} is independent of the current outcome innovation and both are independent of the past, this dependence on yt−1y_{t-1} does not itself invalidate the current outcome equation. The conditioning set already contains that history. Feedback tomorrow is different from correlation with the disturbance today.

Strict exogeneity is stronger. Requiring today’s disturbance to be unrelated to the entire path of xx, including future values, rules out some feedback that our conditional-mean assumption allows. In the feedback example, today’s outcome innovation helps determine yty_t, which enters xt+1x_{t+1}. Future xx therefore contains information about today’s disturbance. We do not need that stronger whole-path assumption merely to state the sequential conditional model.

What Would Not Repair the Problem?

  • Lagging xx automatically. A lag is known earlier, but it may still be related to an omitted persistent driver or a serially dependent disturbance. A lag is a date, not an exogeneity certificate.
  • Adding many lags. This may approximate missing dynamics, but it can also exhaust the sample and create collinearity. It does not establish the missing moment restrictions.
  • A clean residual ACF. This checks a particular implication for residual dependence; it cannot verify that current regressors are uncorrelated with the structural disturbance.
  • Heteroskedasticity/autocorrelation-robust standard errors. These address variance estimation when the coefficient estimator has valid moments and suitable asymptotics. They do not remove inconsistency caused by invalid moments.

A reporting habit. State the goal before interpreting the coefficient: “conditional prediction given this information,” “response along this specified input path,” or “causal response to an intervention.” The last claim requires additional causal assumptions, including a defensible source of variation and a relationship that remains valid under the intervention. The conditional-mean equation alone does not supply them.

Technical Note — Consistency Is Not Exact Finite-Sample Inference

Write yt=zt′ϑ+ϵty_t=z_t'\vartheta+\epsilon_t. The OLS estimation error satisfies

ϑ̂−ϑ=(T−1∑tztzt′)−1(T−1∑tztϵt). \hat\vartheta-\vartheta= \left(T^{-1}\sum_tz_tz_t'\right)^{-1} \left(T^{-1}\sum_tz_t\epsilon_t\right).

Under stationary/ergodic sampling, suitable finite moments, E[ztϵt]=0E[z_t\epsilon_t]=0, and positive definite E[ztzt′]E[z_tz_t'], the second factor converges to zero and the first to a finite matrix. Asymptotic normality and a valid standard error require additional central-limit and variance conditions. Conditional homoskedasticity yields the familiar covariance expression; heteroskedasticity requires an appropriate robust estimate.

Because lagged yy contains earlier disturbances, the full sample regressor matrix is not generally independent of the full disturbance vector. Do not transfer the exact finite-sample unbiasedness and textbook exact t/Ft/F distributions from a strictly exogenous Gaussian regression without checking their conditions. The Core claim is large-sample justification under stated restrictions, not an exact small-sample guarantee.

8.4 Build the DGP, Then Break Its Assumptions — Core

A Persistent Predictor, Not Five Unrelated Columns

We will generate both series, so we know what the outcome coefficients are. Let

xt=0.5xt−1+cyt−1+ϵx,t,yt=0.2+0.6yt−1+0.4xt+0.2xt−1+ϵt. \begin{aligned} x_t&=0.5x_{t-1}+c\,y_{t-1}+\epsilon_{x,t},\\ y_t&=0.2+0.6y_{t-1}+0.4x_t+0.2x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t. \end{aligned}

The symbol cc is the feedback coefficient in this demonstration. The two current shocks have variance one and correlation rr; shock pairs are independent across dates. We vary cc and rr while keeping the structural outcome coefficients fixed.

Case Feedback cc Current-shock correlation rr Prediction before running
Baseline 0 0 OLS should approach the DGP coefficients as the sample grows.
Shared current shocks 0 0.7 Current xx reveals part of the structural disturbance; structural coefficients need not be recovered.
Lagged feedback only 0.2 0 Conditional mean restriction can still hold, despite dependence between future xx and today’s innovation.

All three parameter configurations have stable joint dynamics. In the feedback case the two transition eigenvalues are approximately 0.887 and 0.293, inside one in absolute value. This is the system analogue of the characteristic-root condition, equivalent to lag-polynomial roots outside the unit circle.

The shared-shock case deliberately breaks the innovation interpretation: there ϵt\epsilon_t remains the structural DGP disturbance, but it is no longer an innovation relative to ℱt−1\mathcal F_{t-1} and xtx_t. Keep that distinction in mind when comparing its known coefficients with regression estimates.

Build the Simulator Inline

Run the code in order. It needs the course packages ggplot2 and forecast; the empirical section also uses urca. Cached CSV files make the chapter runnable without a network connection or an API key. The two functions built here have identical canonical copies in helpers/ardl_utils.R for use in later modules.

library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))
Sys.setenv(OMP_NUM_THREADS = "1", OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS = "1",
           MKL_NUM_THREADS = "1")
# Run from the project root or from notes/ (Quarto's default R directory).
data_dir <- if (dir.exists("data")) "data" else "../data"
stopifnot(dir.exists(data_dir))
ardl_simulator <- function(n = 400, alpha = 0.2, phi = 0.6,
                           beta = c(0.4, 0.2), rho_x = 0.5,
                           feedback = 0, shock_corr = 0, burn_in = 200) {
  stopifnot(n >= 2, n == as.integer(n), burn_in >= 0,
            burn_in == as.integer(burn_in), length(beta) == 2,
            all(is.finite(c(alpha, phi, beta, rho_x, feedback, shock_corr))),
            abs(shock_corr) < 1)
  total <- n + burn_in + 1L
  epsilon_x <- rnorm(total)
  epsilon <- shock_corr * epsilon_x +
    sqrt(1 - shock_corr^2) * rnorm(total)
  x <- y <- numeric(total)
  for (t in 2:total) {
    x[t] <- rho_x * x[t - 1] + feedback * y[t - 1] + epsilon_x[t]
    y[t] <- alpha + phi * y[t - 1] + beta[1] * x[t] +
      beta[2] * x[t - 1] + epsilon[t]
  }
  keep <- (burn_in + 2L):total
  data.frame(t = seq_len(n), y = y[keep], x = x[keep],
             epsilon = epsilon[keep], epsilon_x = epsilon_x[keep])
}

The for-loop is the pair of equations. We compute xtx_t first because this DGP specifies it before current yty_t. We then discard a burn-in period so the arbitrary zero starting values have little influence. Burn-in is useful for a stable system; it cannot turn an unstable system into a stationary one.

case_names <- c("Baseline", "Shared current shocks", "Lagged feedback only")
case_corr <- c(0, 0.7, 0)
case_feedback <- c(0, 0, 0.2)
case_data <- case_fits <- vector("list", 3)
single_estimates <- matrix(NA_real_, 3, 4,
                           dimnames = list(case_names,
                                           c("alpha", "phi_1", "beta_0", "beta_1")))
for (s in seq_along(case_names)) {
  set.seed(637608)  # Same underlying independent draws across the three cases.
  d <- ardl_simulator(shock_corr = case_corr[s], feedback = case_feedback[s])
  d$y_lag1 <- c(NA, head(d$y, -1))
  d$x_lag1 <- c(NA, head(d$x, -1))
  fit <- lm(y ~ y_lag1 + x + x_lag1, data = d)
  case_data[[s]] <- d
  case_fits[[s]] <- fit
  single_estimates[s, ] <- coef(fit)
}
knitr::kable(rbind("DGP coefficients" = c(0.2, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2),
                   single_estimates), digits = 3)
alpha phi_1 beta_0 beta_1
DGP coefficients 0.200 0.600 0.400 0.200
Baseline 0.221 0.555 0.352 0.276
Shared current shocks 0.217 0.565 1.065 -0.068
Lagged feedback only 0.265 0.552 0.349 0.259

We construct lags with an explicit missing value at the beginning. This is more transparent than relying on a package’s lag() convention: for a plain numeric vector, stats::lag() changes time attributes rather than necessarily producing the shifted column you intended. lm() drops the first unavailable-lag row here.

One Draw Is Not the Distribution

An estimate can miss the truth through ordinary sampling variation. To see the pattern, repeat the same small experiment. This is a short, serial Monte Carlo: one seed at the beginning, successive random draws, no parallel workers.

set.seed(637609)
B <- 200
mc <- array(NA_real_, c(B, 4, 3),
            dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(single_estimates), case_names))
for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  for (s in seq_along(case_names)) {
    d <- ardl_simulator(shock_corr = case_corr[s], feedback = case_feedback[s])
    d$y_lag1 <- c(NA, head(d$y, -1))
    d$x_lag1 <- c(NA, head(d$x, -1))
    mc[b, , s] <- coef(lm(y ~ y_lag1 + x + x_lag1, data = d))
  }
}
mc_table <- data.frame()
truth <- c(0.2, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2)
for (s in seq_along(case_names)) {
  for (j in seq_along(truth)) {
    mc_table <- rbind(mc_table, data.frame(
      case = case_names[s], coefficient = colnames(single_estimates)[j],
      DGP = truth[j], mean_estimate = mean(mc[, j, s]),
      simulation_sd = sd(mc[, j, s]),
      MCSE_of_mean = sd(mc[, j, s]) / sqrt(B)))
  }
}
knitr::kable(mc_table, digits = 3)
case coefficient DGP mean_estimate simulation_sd MCSE_of_mean
Baseline alpha 0.2 0.204 0.053 0.004
Baseline phi_1 0.6 0.599 0.033 0.002
Baseline beta_0 0.4 0.396 0.053 0.004
Baseline beta_1 0.2 0.206 0.055 0.004
Shared current shocks alpha 0.2 0.205 0.039 0.003
Shared current shocks phi_1 0.6 0.597 0.028 0.002
Shared current shocks beta_0 0.4 1.097 0.036 0.003
Shared current shocks beta_1 0.2 -0.144 0.055 0.004
Lagged feedback only alpha 0.2 0.206 0.058 0.004
Lagged feedback only phi_1 0.6 0.595 0.034 0.002
Lagged feedback only beta_0 0.4 0.403 0.042 0.003
Lagged feedback only beta_1 0.2 0.200 0.053 0.004 
mc_plot <- data.frame(estimate = as.vector(mc[, "beta_0", ]),
                      case = rep(case_names, each = B))
ggplot(mc_plot, aes(x = estimate, fill = case)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.4, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ case, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Estimated contemporaneous coefficient", y = "Replications",
       title = "Same structural beta_0; different regressor–disturbance relations",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: structural DGP coefficient 0.4") +
  guides(fill = "none")

The simulation standard deviation describes variation across samples. The Monte Carlo standard error of the mean describes the numerical precision of this simulation summary. Neither is a correction for estimating the wrong target.

The baseline and feedback-only cases should center near the structural coefficients, with finite-sample error. The shared-shock case should systematically miss some of them. Increasing the sample size makes that discrepancy clearer; it does not make the structural interpretation valid.

Why the Shared-Shock Regression Can Still Look Clean

Because the simulator uses jointly Gaussian shocks with unit variances,

E[ϵt∣ϵx,t]=0.7ϵx,t.E[\epsilon_t\mid\epsilon_{x,t}]=0.7\epsilon_{x,t}.

In the shared-shock case, ϵx,t=xt−0.5xt−1\epsilon_{x,t}=x_t-0.5x_{t-1}. Consequently the conditional mean is

E[yt∣ℱt−1,xt]=0.2+0.6yt−1+1.1xt−0.15xt−1. E[y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t] =0.2+0.6y_{t-1}+1.1x_t-0.15x_{t-1}.

The structural contemporaneous coefficient is 0.4, but the conditional projection coefficient is 0.4+0.7=1.10.4+0.7=1.1. The structural lag coefficient is 0.2, but its conditional counterpart is 0.2−0.7(0.5)=−0.150.2-0.7(0.5)=-0.15. OLS has not randomly malfunctioned: it is estimating a different conditional relationship than the structural one we wanted to interpret.

After accounting for that projection, the remaining disturbance is ϵt−0.7ϵx,t\epsilon_t-0.7\epsilon_{x,t}. In this constructed example it is independent of current xx innovations and serially independent. Residuals can therefore look clean despite failure to recover the structural coefficients.

forecast::ggAcf(residuals(case_fits[[2]]), lag.max = 20) +
  labs(title = "Residual ACF: the shared-shock equation can look well specified",
       subtitle = "A residual diagnostic cannot certify a structural interpretation")

Break it again. Increase the sample size to 2,000 while keeping the shared-shock design. Before running, predict whether β̂0\hat\beta_0 will move toward 0.4 or toward 1.1. Then set shock_corr = 0 and keep feedback = 0.2. Explain why that change is economically different.

Application callback. A current policy rate or current claims measure may both reflect news about the outcome. An empirical coefficient could be a useful conditional association without measuring the causal response to an isolated policy or labor-market intervention. In §8.7 we make a forecasting claim and use dated predictor lags; we do not relabel its coefficients as structural effects.

8.5 How a Change Travels Through the Equation — Core

Specify the Input Experiment First

A distributed lag and an autoregression both spread a change across time. Start with

yt=0.6yt−1+0.4xt+0.2xt−1+ϵt.y_t=0.6y_{t-1}+0.4x_t+0.2x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t.

Compare two paths with the same initial conditions and the same outcome shocks. Change only the imposed xx path. Subtracting the paths cancels the shocks and gives a deterministic recursion for the difference in yy.

There are two different experiments:

  1. Pulse: raise xtx_t by one unit for one period; return later xx values to their baseline path.
  2. Permanent step: raise xt,xt+1,…x_t,x_{t+1},\ldots by one unit in every subsequent period.

These are conditional input experiments. When xx itself has persistence or responds to yy, the imposed path need not be the path generated by a one-unit shock to xx’s own equation. We will distinguish those experiments below.

Impact and Horizon-Specific Pulse Multipliers

Let mhm_h be the difference in yt+hy_{t+h} caused by the imposed one-period unit pulse, holding all other inputs and innovations fixed. In an ARDL(1,1)(1,1),

m0=β0,m1=ϕ1β0+β1,mh=ϕ1mh−1,h≥2. \begin{aligned} m_0&=\beta_0,\\ m_1&=\phi_1\beta_0+\beta_1,\\ m_h&=\phi_1m_{h-1},\qquad h\ge2. \end{aligned}

The impact multiplier is 0.4. One period later the response is 0.6(0.4)+0.2=0.440.6(0.4)+0.2=0.44: part comes through inherited yy, and part through lagged xx. At horizon two it is 0.6(0.44)=0.2640.6(0.44)=0.264.

Thus β1\beta_1 alone is not the total response after one period. It describes one route into the equation, not the sum of all paths in the time-unrolled graph.

Cumulative and Permanent-Step Multipliers

The cumulative pulse response through horizon HH is ∑h=0Hmh\sum_{h=0}^{H}m_h. For this linear, time-invariant equation, that sum also equals the response at horizon HH to a permanent unit step. Some texts call this an interim multiplier; we state “cumulative through HH” to keep the experiment explicit.

Horizon Pulse response mhm_h Permanent-step response ∑j=0hmj\sum_{j=0}^{h}m_j
0 0.4000 0.4000
1 0.4400 0.8400
2 0.2640 1.1040
3 0.1584 1.2624
Long run 0 1.5000

The intercept does not affect these differences because it is the same in both paths. If the outcome is measured in percentage points and the predictor in thousands of claims, the response is in percentage points per additional thousand claims. Units belong in the interpretation.

Long-Run Multiplier

If the conditional outcome dynamics are stable, a permanent unit increase in xx eventually changes yy by

∑ℓ=0qβℓ1−∑j=1pϕj. \boxed{\frac{\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell} {1-\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j}.}

For the numerical example it is (0.4+0.2)/(1−0.6)=1.5(0.4+0.2)/(1-0.6)=1.5. You can obtain this by summing the pulse responses, or by comparing two steady-state equations whose predictor levels differ by one.

This is a long-run change, not the mean of yy. With constant predictor level x‾\bar x, the steady-state level would instead solve y‾=[α+(∑βℓ)x‾]/[1−∑ϕj]\bar y=[\alpha+(\sum\beta_\ell)\bar x]/[1-\sum\phi_j].

Even when the estimated dynamics are stable, a denominator close to zero makes the estimated long-run multiplier sensitive to small coefficient errors. Report that uncertainty rather than treating a large plug-in ratio as a precisely known response. The optional Technical Note below explains why the coefficient estimates must be considered jointly.

Build and Plot the Responses

The following function implements the recursion for any finite AR and predictor lag vectors. beta[1] is β0\beta_0; phi[1] is ϕ1\phi_1.

ardl_multipliers <- function(phi, beta, horizon = 20) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(phi), is.numeric(beta), length(beta) >= 1,
            all(is.finite(c(phi, beta))), horizon >= 0,
            horizon == as.integer(horizon))
  pulse <- numeric(horizon + 1L)
  for (h in 0:horizon) {
    direct <- if (h < length(beta)) beta[h + 1L] else 0
    inherited <- 0
    if (h > 0 && length(phi) > 0) {
      for (j in seq_len(min(length(phi), h))) {
        inherited <- inherited + phi[j] * pulse[h - j + 1L]
      }
    }
    pulse[h + 1L] <- direct + inherited
  }
  data.frame(h = 0:horizon, pulse = pulse, step = cumsum(pulse))
}
response <- ardl_multipliers(phi = 0.6, beta = c(0.4, 0.2), horizon = 20)
knitr::kable(head(response, 5), digits = 4)
h pulse step
0 0.4000 0.4000
1 0.4400 0.8400
2 0.2640 1.1040
3 0.1584 1.2624
4 0.0950 1.3574 
response_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(h = response$h, response = response$pulse, experiment = "Pulse"),
  data.frame(h = response$h, response = response$step, experiment = "Permanent step"))
ggplot(response_long, aes(h, response, color = experiment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.7) +
  labs(x = "Periods since the imposed change", y = "Difference in y",
       color = "Input path", title = "One equation, two different input experiments") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

A second worked example. Keep the direct predictor effects fixed but set ϕ1=−0.5\phi_1=-0.5. Then m0=0.4m_0=0.4, m1=−0.5(0.4)+0.2=0m_1=-0.5(0.4)+0.2=0, and all later pulse responses are zero. The long-run step response is 0.6/1.5=0.40.6/1.5=0.4. A positive lag coefficient and negative autoregressive propagation exactly offset at horizon one. You cannot infer the response shape by reading the signs of the β\beta coefficients alone.

Break Stability

stable <- ardl_multipliers(0.6, c(0.4, 0.2), horizon = 20)
unit_root <- ardl_multipliers(1, c(0.4, 0.2), horizon = 20)
unstable <- ardl_multipliers(1.05, c(0.4, 0.2), horizon = 20)
break_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(h = stable$h, step = stable$step, phi = "phi = 0.6"),
  data.frame(h = unit_root$h, step = unit_root$step, phi = "phi = 1"),
  data.frame(h = unstable$h, step = unstable$step, phi = "phi = 1.05"))
ggplot(break_plot, aes(h, step, color = phi)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Periods since permanent step", y = "Difference in y",
       color = NULL, title = "A formula needs its stability condition") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

At ϕ1=1\phi_1=1, the pulse leaves a lasting increment, so repeated increments from a permanent step accumulate. At ϕ1=1.05\phi_1=1.05, the denominator in the algebraic ratio is nonzero, but the response does not converge. A nonzero denominator is not a substitute for stability. Reporting 0.6/(1−1.05)=−120.6/(1-1.05)=-12 as the eventual response would contradict the path we just computed.

An Innovation to Persistent xx Is a Different Experiment

In the baseline design with independent current shocks and no feedback, let xt=0.5xt−1+ϵx,tx_t=0.5x_{t-1}+\epsilon_{x,t}. An isolated unit innovation to xx, holding the outcome-shock path fixed, produces the input path 1,0.5,0.25,…1,0.5,0.25,\ldots. Its outcome response at horizon one is therefore 0.44+0.4(0.5)=0.640.44+0.4(0.5)=0.64, not the pulse response 0.44. Later responses combine the ARDL pulse multipliers with the entire innovation-induced xx path. With shared current shocks, conditioning on an xx innovation can also change the expected outcome disturbance: 0.64 then describes only the mechanical input-path contribution. With feedback, one must follow both equations jointly.

This is why a conditional multiplier is not automatically a structural impulse response. A causal intervention is a further interpretation requiring assumptions that justify changing one mechanism while holding others fixed. A fitted equation by itself does not establish that invariance.

Application callback. If §8.7 models monthly changes in the unemployment rate against growth in claims, a “permanent step in xx” means permanently higher claims growth, not a once-and-for-all increase in the level of claims. Always translate the multiplier experiment back through the transformations before making an economic statement.

Deeper Dive — The General Recursion

Set βh=0\beta_h=0 for h>qh>q and mh=0m_h=0 for h<0h<0. Equating the difference between two outcome paths gives

mh=βh+∑j=1pϕjmh−j.m_h=\beta_h+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_jm_{h-j}.

The first term is the direct contribution of the original pulse through the distributed lag. The sum is its inherited contribution through past outcome responses. If the responses are absolutely summable, summing both sides over h≥0h\ge0 yields

∑h=0∞mh=∑ℓ=0qβℓ+(∑j=1pϕj)∑h=0∞mh,\sum_{h=0}^{\infty}m_h =\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell+ \left(\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j\right)\sum_{h=0}^{\infty}m_h,

which gives the long-run multiplier. This also shows why simply summing the direct β\beta coefficients misses autoregressive propagation.

Technical Note — An Estimated Ratio Has Uncertainty

Replacing coefficients by estimates gives m̂h\hat m_h and an estimated long-run multiplier. They are estimates, not known DGP responses. The long-run ratio can be particularly unstable when 1−∑jϕ̂j1-\sum_j\hat\phi_j is close to zero. Uncertainty depends on the joint covariance of the estimated AR and predictor coefficients, not only their separate standard errors. Delta-method or suitable bootstrap calculations are possible under their own regularity conditions; we do not use a plug-in ratio as its own confidence statement.

8.6 Estimation, Diagnostics, and Forecast Timing — Core

Extend the Familiar Workflow

The practical sequence is still specify → estimate → diagnose → revise → evaluate. The new tasks are to justify predictor timing and to keep the goal of the equation explicit.

  1. Inspect and transform. Establish units, frequency, seasonal adjustment, release timing, and whether the stationary baseline is appropriate.
  2. Choose a modest candidate lag set. Use economic timing and the sampling frequency to bound the search. ACF/PACF patterns of yy alone cannot determine all cross-variable lags.
  3. Build and inspect the lag columns. Verify that a regressor labelled xt−1x_{t-1} actually refers to the previous observation on the intended calendar.
  4. Use a common estimation sample. Candidate models with different maximum lags otherwise lose different initial observations. Information criteria must compare the same outcomes under the same likelihood convention.
  5. Estimate, then diagnose. A lower BIC does not certify correct timing, exogeneity, or a stable relationship.
  6. Evaluate the intended use. For forecasting, score predictions made without future information on the same dates as the benchmark.

A Common-Sample Lag Comparison

We first use the baseline simulated data, where the maintained assumptions are known. The real-data section repeats this workflow with the complications of an observed economic series.

d <- case_data[[1]]
for (j in 1:3) {
  d[[paste0("y_lag", j)]] <- c(rep(NA_real_, j), head(d$y, -j))
  d[[paste0("x_lag", j)]] <- c(rep(NA_real_, j), head(d$x, -j))
}
d_common <- d[complete.cases(d), ]  # All candidates lose the same three rows.
candidate_grid <- expand.grid(p = 1:3, q = 0:3)
candidate_grid$BIC <- NA_real_
candidate_fits <- vector("list", nrow(candidate_grid))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(candidate_grid))) {
  p <- candidate_grid$p[i]
  q <- candidate_grid$q[i]
  rhs <- c(paste0("y_lag", seq_len(p)), "x")
  if (q > 0) rhs <- c(rhs, paste0("x_lag", seq_len(q)))
  fit <- lm(reformulate(rhs, response = "y"), data = d_common)
  candidate_fits[[i]] <- fit
  candidate_grid$BIC[i] <- BIC(fit)
}
knitr::kable(candidate_grid[order(candidate_grid$BIC), ], digits = 2)
p q BIC
4 1 1 1164.42
5 2 1 1169.62
7 1 2 1170.05
10 1 3 1173.59
6 3 1 1175.01
8 2 2 1175.39
11 2 3 1177.34
9 3 2 1180.70
1 1 0 1181.31
12 3 3 1182.00
2 2 0 1185.26
3 3 0 1190.45 
selected_fit <- candidate_fits[[which.min(candidate_grid$BIC)]]
knitr::kable(coef(summary(selected_fit)), digits = 3)
Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 0.223 0.055 4.070 0
y_lag1 0.556 0.036 15.518 0
x 0.354 0.052 6.823 0
x_lag1 0.274 0.057 4.828 0

In a finite sample, an information criterion may select a model other than the DGP specification. Its penalty trades fit against complexity; it is not an oracle. In BIC(lm(...)), the likelihood parameter count includes the regression coefficients and an estimated disturbance variance, as in Module 4.

Persistent xx values can make adjacent lag columns highly correlated. Their individual coefficients may then be imprecise even when the predictor block contributes useful information. Do not drop one lag solely because its individual tt statistic is small, without considering the joint lag structure and the intended forecast.

Residual Diagnostics for a Dynamic Regression

Plot the residuals, inspect their ACF, and ask whether the remaining structure points to missing dynamics or instability. A regression-appropriate serial-correlation check is the Breusch–Godfrey auxiliary regression: regress the fitted residual on the original regressors and several of its own lags. If those residual lags add predictive information, the fitted equation has left serial dependence behind.

residual_frame <- data.frame(t = d_common$t, e = residuals(selected_fit))
ggplot(residual_frame, aes(t, e)) + geom_line(color = "#315375") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Fitted residual", title = "Does the fitted equation leave structure?")
forecast::ggAcf(residual_frame$e, lag.max = 20) +
  labs(title = "Residual ACF of the selected simulated ARDL")
# Visible Breusch–Godfrey-style auxiliary regression, using four residual lags.
bg_lags <- 4L
bg_frame <- data.frame(e = residuals(selected_fit),
                       model.matrix(selected_fit)[, -1, drop = FALSE])
for (j in seq_len(bg_lags)) {
  bg_frame[[paste0("e_lag", j)]] <-
    c(rep(NA_real_, j), head(bg_frame$e, -j))
}
bg_frame <- bg_frame[complete.cases(bg_frame), ]
bg_fit <- lm(e ~ ., data = bg_frame)
bg_stat <- nobs(bg_fit) * summary(bg_fit)$r.squared
c(LM = bg_stat, df = bg_lags,
  approximate_p = pchisq(bg_stat, df = bg_lags, lower.tail = FALSE))
           LM            df approximate_p 
    4.0107116     4.0000000     0.4045581

Under the null and the usual stationary regression regularity and variance conditions, the LM statistic has an asymptotic χ2\chi^2 reference with degrees of freedom equal to the number of residual lags tested. This is an approximate diagnostic, not an exact small-sample certificate. The first four residual-lag rows were omitted consistently in the auxiliary regression.

Do not mechanically reuse an ARMA-specific Ljung–Box degrees-of-freedom correction for an ARDL. More fundamentally, neither this test nor a residual ACF establishes the relation between the regressors and the structural disturbance. The shared-shock simulation already showed the limit of that reasoning.

Break the specification. Refit the baseline simulated data with lm(y ~ x, data = d_common) and repeat the residual ACF. Predict the omitted paths in the diagram before plotting. If outcome lags belong in the conditional mean, leaving them out can move both coefficient estimates and residual dependence; a standard-error adjustment does not restore the missing dynamics.

The New Predictor Creates a New Forecasting Problem

For a correctly specified ARDL(1,1)(1,1), a one-step forecast made at time tt takes the form

ỹt+1∣t=α̂+ϕ̂1yt+β̂0x̃t+1∣t+β̂1xt. \tilde y_{t+1\mid t} =\hat\alpha+\hat\phi_1y_t+ \hat\beta_0\tilde x_{t+1\mid t}+\hat\beta_1x_t.

The new object is x̃t+1∣t\tilde x_{t+1\mid t}. If current xx enters the outcome equation, a future outcome generally requires a future predictor value. There are several ways to proceed, each answering a different question.

Available information Interpretation
Only observed predictor lags enter the one-step equation Forecast from already available history
Current predictor released before the current target outcome Nowcast using additional within-period information
A stipulated future path for xx Conditional/scenario forecast
Future xx is unknown and must be predicted Forecast requiring a predictor model, possibly a joint system

An ARDL with β0=0\beta_0=0 avoids needing future xx for a one-step forecast only if its lagged variables are actually released at the forecast origin. Longer horizons may still require forecasts of xx.

A Timestamp Is Not a Release Date

Suppose a dataset labels an observation “October.” That may mean it measures October, not that it was available on October 1 or October 31. A forecast must use the information available on the date it is issued.

Reference period:       September              October
Calendar:       ----------------------|---------------------------->
                                      previous-month data released
                                      ^ possible forecast origin
                                                  target-month release later

A forecast of October unemployment made after September data are released can use September variables. It cannot use October information that arrives later simply because all rows are now sitting in one CSV file. Weekly claims also require an explicit aggregation rule before they can become a monthly regressor.

Conditional and Predictor Uncertainty

If the future xx path were known, forecast uncertainty would still include future outcome disturbances and estimated-coefficient uncertainty. If that path is itself estimated, an honest unconditional forecast interval must account for predictor uncertainty and any relevant dependence between predictor and outcome forecast errors. Treating a point forecast of xx as if it were known generally understates what is uncertain.

For example, even with known coefficients, the one-step error contains β0(xt+1−x̃t+1∣t)+ϵt+1\beta_0(x_{t+1}-\tilde x_{t+1\mid t})+\epsilon_{t+1}. Its variance includes a predictor-error variance term and, when present, a covariance term. A scenario band conditional on a specified xx path omits those terms by design; label it accordingly.

Forecast availability experiment. In the baseline simulation, the following comparison deliberately gives one method future information. It illustrates how easily a favorable score can answer the wrong question.

set.seed(637610)
forecast_data <- ardl_simulator(n = 800)
forecast_data$y_lag1 <- c(NA, head(forecast_data$y, -1))
forecast_data$x_lag1 <- c(NA, head(forecast_data$x, -1))
train <- forecast_data[2:600, ]
holdout <- forecast_data[601:800, ]
forecast_fit <- lm(y ~ y_lag1 + x + x_lag1, data = train)
x_fit <- lm(x ~ x_lag1, data = train)
feasible_inputs <- holdout
feasible_inputs$x <- predict(x_fit, newdata = holdout)
feasible <- predict(forecast_fit, newdata = feasible_inputs)
oracle <- predict(forecast_fit, newdata = holdout)  # Knows target-period x.
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  information = c("Forecast x from its observed lag", "Oracle: observe target-period x"),
  RMSE = c(sqrt(mean((holdout$y - feasible)^2)),
           sqrt(mean((holdout$y - oracle)^2)))), digits = 3)
information RMSE
Forecast x from its observed lag 1.039
Oracle: observe target-period x 0.950

Both methods keep estimated coefficients fixed and roll the observed lag information forward. The oracle has an informational advantage that a genuine earlier forecast does not have. Calling its score an ordinary out-of-sample forecasting gain would be leakage. It could instead be a legitimate nowcast score if the predictor really were available first; the release calendar decides.

8.7 Real Data — Do Initial Claims Add Usable Information? — Core

Module 7 ended with a limitation: combining forecasts can reshuffle the information in a pool, but every member of our pool used unemployment’s own history. Initial unemployment-insurance claims offer a plausible additional signal. More people entering the claims system may warn us that labor-market conditions are deteriorating. Whether that signal improves a particular forecast is an empirical question.

Define the variables before fitting anything

Let UtU_t denote the monthly U.S. unemployment rate, measured in percent, and let CtC_t denote the mean of the weekly initial-claims observations whose week-ending Saturdays fall in month tt. Both source series are seasonally adjusted. UtU_t comes from the household survey; claims are administrative records of initial benefit applications, so these are related labor-market measures with different populations and definitions. See FRED’s UNRATE metadata and FRED’s ICSA metadata.

We model

yt=ΔUt,xt=100ΔlogCt.y_t=\Delta U_t,\qquad x_t=100\Delta\log C_t.

The outcome is a change in percentage points. The predictor is a log change multiplied by 100, approximately the percentage change in the monthly mean of weekly claims. Averaging four or five weekly counts does not create a monthly total. We assign a week crossing a month boundary to the month containing its Saturday, and use that convention consistently.

These transformations give us a stationary working specification to investigate. They do not declare that both original series are necessarily I(1)I(1) in every sample, or that differencing automatically solves specification problems. We check the transformed series on training data before using ordinary stationary-regression reasoning.

The timing contract matters. A month’s label is its reference period, not its publication date. BLS usually releases the unemployment rate early in the following month; the BLS definitions distinguish reference, interview, and release dates. The DOL weekly claims release likewise reports a completed week after its Saturday ending date.

For this exercise, the forecast origin is after both the previous month’s unemployment release and the release covering its final claims Saturday have arrived, but before the target month’s unemployment release. Thus, when forecasting yty_t, we use yt−1y_{t-1} and xt−1x_{t-1} and their earlier lags. We deliberately ignore partial target-month claims. This is one step ahead in the monthly observation index, and ordinarily a nowcast of the current calendar month; it is not a forecast made at the end of the preceding calendar month. We write its information set as ℐtrelease\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}} and its forecast as ỹt∣ℐtrelease\tilde y_{t\mid\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}} to keep that distinction visible.

The cached observations are revised historical data, not releases archived at each forecast origin. The unemployment and claims caches were also collected on different dates. Our exercise therefore isolates temporal fitting and evaluation on a revised-data pseudo-out-of-sample basis. It does not reproduce a real-time forecaster’s historical data vintages or exact release calendar. A real deployment must check the releases actually available at its origin, especially during delays, and use a vintage archive to evaluate real-time performance.

Retrieve once, then work offline

The live retrieval is shown for students with a FRED key. It is not executed when the notes render. The stored claims cache covers 1989–2019; 1989 supplies the pre-sample observations needed for differences and lags. The existing unemployment cache is left unchanged.

library(fredr)
fredr_set_key(Sys.getenv("FRED_KEY"))
claims_live <- fredr(
  series_id = "ICSA",
  observation_start = as.Date("1989-01-01"),
  observation_end = as.Date("2019-12-31")
)
unemployment_live <- fredr(
  series_id = "UNRATE",
  observation_start = as.Date("1988-12-01"),
  observation_end = as.Date("2019-12-31")
)

Load the frozen files and check their calendars before merging. Missing weeks cannot be silently dropped from a monthly mean, and missing months cannot be silently treated as adjacent observations.

app_u <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "UNRATE.csv"))
app_c <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "ICSA.csv"))
app_u$observation_date <- as.Date(app_u$observation_date)
app_c$observation_date <- as.Date(app_c$observation_date)
app_u <- app_u[app_u$observation_date >= as.Date("1988-12-01") &
                 app_u$observation_date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"), ]
app_c <- app_c[order(app_c$observation_date), ]
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(app_u), !anyNA(app_c), all(app_c$ICSA > 0),
  !anyDuplicated(app_c$observation_date),
  all(as.POSIXlt(app_c$observation_date)$wday == 6),
  identical(app_c$observation_date,
            seq(as.Date("1989-01-07"), as.Date("2019-12-28"), by = "week")),
  identical(app_u$observation_date,
            seq(as.Date("1988-12-01"), as.Date("2019-12-01"), by = "month"))
)
# December 1988 unemployment supplies January 1989's change;
# this makes twelve outcome lags available by January 1990.
app_u$y <- c(NA_real_, diff(app_u$UNRATE))
app_u$U_previous <- c(NA_real_, head(app_u$UNRATE, -1L))
app_u <- app_u[app_u$observation_date >= as.Date("1989-01-01"), ]
app_c$month <- as.Date(format(app_c$observation_date, "%Y-%m-01"))
app_month_c <- aggregate(ICSA ~ month, data = app_c, FUN = mean)
app_nweeks <- table(app_c$month)
stopifnot(all(app_nweeks %in% c(4L, 5L)))
app_data <- merge(app_u, app_month_c,
                  by.x = "observation_date", by.y = "month", all = TRUE)
names(app_data)[match(c("observation_date", "UNRATE", "ICSA"),
                      names(app_data))] <- c("date", "U", "C")
stopifnot(nrow(app_data) == 372L, !anyNA(app_data))
app_data$x <- c(NA_real_, 100 * diff(log(app_data$C)))
for (j in 1:12) {
  app_data[[paste0("y_l", j)]] <-
    c(rep(NA_real_, j), head(app_data$y, -j))
  if (j <= 3) {
    app_data[[paste0("x_l", j)]] <-
      c(rep(NA_real_, j), head(app_data$x, -j))
  }
}
app_data <- app_data[app_data$date >= as.Date("1990-01-01"), ]
stopifnot(nrow(app_data) == 360L, !anyNA(app_data))
app_train <- app_data[app_data$date <= as.Date("2017-12-01"), ]
app_test <- app_data[app_data$date >= as.Date("2018-01-01"), ]
stopifnot(nrow(app_train) == 336L, nrow(app_test) == 24L)

Training runs from January 1990 through December 2017. January 2018 through December 2019 is held out, before the pandemic’s extraordinary disruption. We fix the candidate models and selection rule before looking at that holdout. Restricting the illustration to this period limits its scope; it does not establish that the same model would work through 2020 or in every business-cycle phase.

app_paths <- rbind(
  data.frame(date = app_train$date, value = app_train$U,
             series = "Unemployment rate (percent)"),
  data.frame(date = app_train$date, value = app_train$C / 1000,
             series = "Mean weekly claims (thousands)"),
  data.frame(date = app_train$date, value = app_train$y,
             series = "y: change in unemployment (percentage points)"),
  data.frame(date = app_train$date, value = app_train$x,
             series = "x: 100 times log change in mean weekly claims")
)
ggplot(app_paths, aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#16697A", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ series, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_bw()

From Module 2, the ADF null is a unit root, while the KPSS null here is stationarity around a constant. Use a drift in the ADF regression, choose its augmentation lag by BIC from a maximum of 12, and use 12 lags in the KPSS long-run variance estimate. These choices are stated in advance rather than varied until a preferred conclusion appears.

app_stationarity <- data.frame()
for (app_name in c("y", "x")) {
  app_adf <- urca::ur.df(app_train[[app_name]], type = "drift",
                       lags = 12, selectlags = "BIC")
  app_kpss <- urca::ur.kpss(app_train[[app_name]], type = "mu", use.lag = 12)
  app_stationarity <- rbind(app_stationarity, data.frame(
    Series = app_name,
    ADF_statistic = unname(app_adf@teststat[1, "tau2"]),
    ADF_5pct = unname(app_adf@cval["tau2", "5pct"]),
    KPSS_statistic = unname(app_kpss@teststat),
    KPSS_5pct = unname(app_kpss@cval[1, "5pct"])
  ))
}
knitr::kable(app_stationarity, digits = 3)
Series ADF_statistic ADF_5pct KPSS_statistic KPSS_5pct
y -3.692 -2.87 0.149 0.463
x -12.795 -2.87 0.105 0.463

Reject the ADF null when its statistic is more negative than its critical value; reject the KPSS null when its statistic is larger than its critical value. Here the training-sample evidence is consistent with treating both transformed series as stationary: both ADF tests reject at 5%, and neither KPSS test rejects. These finite-sample tests and plots support a working specification, not a proof of stationarity, exogeneity, constant variance, or stability across future regimes.

Compare a small AR with a lag-only ARDL

The benchmark uses pp own lags. The larger information set adds qq claims lags:

yt=α+∑j=1pϕjyt−j+∑ℓ=1qβℓxt−ℓ+ϵt.y_t=\alpha+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j y_{t-j} +\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\beta_\ell x_{t-\ell}+\epsilon_t.

There is no current xtx_t term. This is the earlier ARDL with the contemporaneous coefficient constrained to zero. It avoids needing a complete target-month claims average at our origin. It does not establish that lagged claims are structurally exogenous: omitted persistent labor-market shocks could still matter.

We consider p=1,2,3p=1,2,3 and q=1,2,3q=1,2,3 for the ARDL and p=1,2,3p=1,2,3 for the AR benchmark. Every candidate uses the same 336 training rows. BIC selects one model within each family; the holdout selects neither lags nor coefficients. In the code, q = 0 is merely the table label for an AR with no claims term, not an ARDL containing current claims.

app_grid <- expand.grid(p = 1:3, q = 0:3)
app_grid$family <- ifelse(app_grid$q == 0, "AR", "ARDL")
app_grid$AIC <- app_grid$BIC <- NA_real_
app_fits <- vector("list", nrow(app_grid))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(app_grid))) {
  app_terms <- paste0("y_l", seq_len(app_grid$p[i]))
  if (app_grid$q[i] > 0) {
    app_terms <- c(app_terms, paste0("x_l", seq_len(app_grid$q[i])))
  }
  app_fits[[i]] <- lm(reformulate(app_terms, response = "y"),
                      data = app_train, na.action = na.fail)
  app_grid$AIC[i] <- AIC(app_fits[[i]])
  app_grid$BIC[i] <- BIC(app_fits[[i]])
  stopifnot(nobs(app_fits[[i]]) == nrow(app_train))
}
app_ar_rows <- which(app_grid$family == "AR")
app_ardl_rows <- which(app_grid$family == "ARDL")
app_ar_row <- app_ar_rows[which.min(app_grid$BIC[app_ar_rows])]
app_ardl_row <- app_ardl_rows[which.min(app_grid$BIC[app_ardl_rows])]
app_ar <- app_fits[[app_ar_row]]
app_ardl <- app_fits[[app_ardl_row]]
app_grid$selected <- seq_len(nrow(app_grid)) %in%
  c(app_ar_row, app_ardl_row)
knitr::kable(app_grid[order(app_grid$family, app_grid$BIC),
                     c("family", "p", "q", "AIC", "BIC", "selected")],
             digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
family p q AIC BIC selected

The selected benchmark has p=p= 3; the selected ARDL has p=p= 3 and q=q= 3. AIC() and BIC() for lm count the innovation variance as a parameter, consistent with the course’s information-criterion convention. BIC measures penalized in-sample fit under its likelihood convention; it does not guarantee a win on future observations.

app_coef <- data.frame(
  Term = names(coef(app_ardl)),
  Estimate = unname(coef(app_ardl)),
  Conventional_SE = unname(sqrt(diag(vcov(app_ardl))))
)

(Intercept) -0.0008 0.0076
y_l1 -0.0523 0.0531
y_l2 0.1120 0.0515
y_l3 0.1823 0.0513

x_l2 0.0093 0.0020

For example, x_l1 estimates β̂1=\hat\beta_1= 0.0069: a one-unit increase in xt−1x_{t-1}—approximately one percentage point faster claims growth—is associated with that many percentage points of predicted unemployment-rate change, holding the other included lags fixed. It is not an estimate of the effect of forcing people to file claims. The conventional standard errors presume the usual variance conditions and do not account for lag selection; we do not promote their ratios into post-selection causal tests.

Diagnose before celebrating fit

The multiplier formula also needs care after transformation: a permanent step in xtx_t means permanently faster claims growth, not one extra claimant or a fixed increase in the claims level. The corresponding response is in unemployment-rate changes. We keep the simple level-path multiplier calculations in the simulation and use this observational application for prediction and diagnostics.

Plot the selected model’s training residuals and their ACF. A persistent pattern means the chosen short lag structure has left information behind.

app_residuals <- data.frame(date = app_train$date, e = residuals(app_ardl))
ggplot(app_residuals, aes(date, e)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey65") +
  geom_line(colour = "#16697A", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual (percentage points)") + theme_bw()
forecast::ggAcf(app_residuals$e, lag.max = 24) + theme_bw()

The following Breusch–Godfrey auxiliary regression tests for residual serial correlation through lag 12. Regress the OLS residuals on the original regressors and twelve residual lags, drop the same first twelve rows for that auxiliary regression, and use its effective sample size times R2R^2. The chi-squared reference is asymptotic and depends on the maintained regression conditions; this is a diagnostic rather than an exogeneity test.

app_bg_data <- app_train
app_bg_data$e <- as.numeric(residuals(app_ardl))
for (j in 1:12) {
  app_bg_data[[paste0("e_l", j)]] <-
    c(rep(NA_real_, j), head(app_bg_data$e, -j))
}
app_bg_data <- app_bg_data[13:nrow(app_bg_data), ]
app_bg_terms <- c(attr(terms(app_ardl), "term.labels"), paste0("e_l", 1:12))
app_bg_fit <- lm(reformulate(app_bg_terms, response = "e"), data = app_bg_data)
app_bg_stat <- nobs(app_bg_fit) * summary(app_bg_fit)$r.squared
app_bg_p <- pchisq(app_bg_stat, df = 12, lower.tail = FALSE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Test = "BG, residual lags 1 through 12",
                       Statistic = app_bg_stat, df = 12,
                       p_value = format.pval(app_bg_p, digits = 3)),
             digits = 4)
Test Statistic df p_value
BG, residual lags 1 through 12 45.4938 12 8.48e-06

The diagnostic pp-value is 8.48e-06. It rejects at 5%, so this short specification leaves evidence of serial dependence. Treat the forecast comparison below as an evaluation of an imperfect candidate, and revisit the lag range or dynamics using training data before deployment. Heteroskedasticity and structural change remain separate concerns. Improving standard errors would not remove an omitted dynamic term or an endogenous regressor.

One disciplined revision using training data

The small-grid winner is not the end of the workflow. It selects the largest allowed own-lag and claims-lag orders, and its residual diagnostics reject the short specification. Make one substantive expansion: allow up to twelve monthly outcome lags, keeping the claims lag maximum at three. Twelve gives the outcome a full year of memory; it does not assert that the already seasonally adjusted series needs seasonal differencing. Expand the AR benchmark’s own-lag menu too. All candidates still use the same 336 training observations, and BIC remains the selection rule. No forecast error from 2018–2019 enters this revision.

app_short_ardl <- app_ardl
app_short_bg_p <- app_bg_p
app_expanded <- expand.grid(p = 1:12, q = 0:3)
app_expanded$family <- ifelse(app_expanded$q == 0, "AR", "ARDL")
app_expanded$BIC <- NA_real_
app_expanded_fits <- vector("list", nrow(app_expanded))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(app_expanded))) {
  app_terms <- paste0("y_l", seq_len(app_expanded$p[i]))
  if (app_expanded$q[i] > 0) {
    app_terms <- c(app_terms, paste0("x_l", seq_len(app_expanded$q[i])))
  }
  app_expanded_fits[[i]] <- lm(reformulate(app_terms, response = "y"),
                               data = app_train, na.action = na.fail)
  app_expanded$BIC[i] <- BIC(app_expanded_fits[[i]])
  stopifnot(nobs(app_expanded_fits[[i]]) == nrow(app_train))
}
app_exp_ar_rows <- which(app_expanded$family == "AR")
app_exp_ardl_rows <- which(app_expanded$family == "ARDL")
app_exp_ar_row <- app_exp_ar_rows[which.min(app_expanded$BIC[app_exp_ar_rows])]
app_exp_ardl_row <- app_exp_ardl_rows[which.min(app_expanded$BIC[app_exp_ardl_rows])]
app_ar <- app_expanded_fits[[app_exp_ar_row]]
app_ardl <- app_expanded_fits[[app_exp_ardl_row]]
# Show each family's three smallest training BIC values.
app_show_rows <- c(
  head(app_exp_ar_rows[order(app_expanded$BIC[app_exp_ar_rows])], 3),
  head(app_exp_ardl_rows[order(app_expanded$BIC[app_exp_ardl_rows])], 3)
)

The revised choices are AR(6) and a lag-only ARDL with p=p= 6 and q=q= 3. Its smallest AR lag-polynomial root modulus is 1.141; values above one satisfy the course’s AR stability condition. The revised BG pp-value is 0.0031. Serial dependence remains detectable at 5%. Stop this illustration here and report that limitation; do not keep changing the model until the diagnostic becomes insignificant. Both the expanded menu and the diagnostic use training data only. Repeated testing and choosing the specification from the same data make these pp-values exploratory checks, not untouched confirmatory evidence.

The forecast comparison now uses these two revised, training-selected specifications. The earlier coefficient table described the initial short model; coefficients in the revised model can differ because its conditioning set has changed.

app_revised_coef <- data.frame(Term = names(coef(app_ardl)),
                               Estimate = unname(coef(app_ardl)))
