Roll the information set, keep the coefficients fixed

The first evaluation origin uses observations through December 2017 once those data have been released. As January 2018 is subsequently released, it becomes an observed lag for the February forecast. The coefficients remain those estimated from the training window. Calling predict() on the held-out rows is safe here because the formulas refer only to lag columns: the target month’s y, x, and unemployment level are never regressors.

For either model,

Ũt∣ℐtrelease=Ut−1+ỹt∣ℐtrelease.\tilde U_{t\mid\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}} =U_{t-1}+\tilde y_{t\mid\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}}.

Add each predicted change to the latest observed unemployment level. Do not accumulate all 24 predicted changes from December 2017: that would be a different, recursive multi-step exercise. A no-change forecast for UtU_t corresponds to forecasting yt=0y_t=0.

app_pred <- data.frame(
  AR = as.numeric(predict(app_ar, newdata = app_test)),
  ARDL = as.numeric(predict(app_ardl, newdata = app_test)),
  No_change = rep(0, nrow(app_test))
)
app_scores <- data.frame()
app_forecast_paths <- data.frame()
for (app_model in names(app_pred)) {
  app_error <- app_test$y - app_pred[[app_model]]
  app_level_forecast <- app_test$U_previous + app_pred[[app_model]]
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(app_error,
                            app_test$U - app_level_forecast)))
  app_scores <- rbind(app_scores, data.frame(
    Model = app_model, N = length(app_error),
    RMSE = sqrt(mean(app_error^2)), MAE = mean(abs(app_error))
  ))
  app_forecast_paths <- rbind(app_forecast_paths, data.frame(
    date = app_test$date, U = app_level_forecast, Model = app_model
  ))
}
knitr::kable(app_scores, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
Model N RMSE MAE
AR 24 0.1129 0.0929
ARDL 24 0.1057 0.0831
No_change 24 0.1099 0.0875

RMSE and MAE have units of unemployment percentage points. They are identical whether calculated for changes or the reconstructed one-step levels because the same observed Ut−1U_{t-1} is added to both sides. MAPE is inappropriate for changes that can be zero or negative, so it is omitted.

ggplot(app_forecast_paths, aes(date, U, colour = Model, linetype = Model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = app_test, aes(date, U), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = app_test, aes(date, U), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             colour = "black", size = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(AR = "#16697A", ARDL = "#D1495B",
                                 No_change = "#8A7B37")) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(c("2018-01-01", "2018-07-01",
                                "2019-01-01", "2019-07-01")),
               date_labels = "%Y-%m") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Unemployment rate (percent)",
       subtitle = "Black line and points: actual unemployment rate") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

On these 24 dates, the selected ARDL’s RMSE is 0.1057, compared with 0.1129 for the selected AR and 0.1099 for carrying the last unemployment rate forward. The ARDL has the lower RMSE than the AR in this particular window. A short holdout ranking is descriptive evidence about these specifications and dates, not a universal ranking of univariate and multivariate models. We do not use it to retune the lag orders and then report the same dates as untouched test data.

What have we learned about exogeneity? Even a forecast improvement would establish neither a policy effect of claims nor the absence of omitted labor-market shocks. Lagged claims can be a useful signal without being an externally controlled input. Our evidence consists of training diagnostics and forecast errors under a stated information convention. A structural interpretation would need an additional argument about the disturbance and the stability of the relationship under the proposed intervention.

Check Your Understanding
  1. Why is averaging weekly claims different from constructing a monthly total? What happens if the final Saturday is missing?
  2. Why is the forecast origin later than the last day of month t−1t-1? Which data would be unavailable if we moved the origin to that day?
  3. Interpret a coefficient of 0.01 on x_l1, stating both units and the conditioning variables. Which causal claim would go beyond it?
  4. Why do the change and reconstructed-level RMSEs match? Why would a 24-month recursive forecast be different?
  5. If claims improve the training BIC but not holdout RMSE, which result should determine a claim about performance on the holdout? Does either result establish exogeneity?

8.8 Looking Ahead — Granger Causality

The forecast exercise asks whether another variable supplies useful information. Granger causality formalizes a related question: does the past of xx improve prediction of yy beyond the past information already being used?

For a first linear stationary illustration, use only lagged predictors:

yt=α+∑j=1pϕjyt−j+∑ℓ=1qβℓxt−ℓ+ϵt. y_t=\alpha+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_jy_{t-j} +\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\beta_\ell x_{t-\ell}+\epsilon_t.

The null of no incremental linear predictive content from those xx lags is

H0:β1=⋯=βq=0.H_0:\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_q=0.

It is a joint restriction: one insignificant lag coefficient is not a test of the entire predictor history. Module 9 develops the restricted/unrestricted comparison, its assumptions, and tests in both directions.

The conditioning set matters. Including current xtx_t and then testing the lag coefficients asks whether past xx adds information conditional on current xx. That is a different information-set question from the usual forecast based on the past. This is why the first Granger example omits the contemporaneous term.

Return to the graph. An arrow from past xx to current yy can describe predictive precedence. It does not tell us whether xx is a direct causal driver, an early indicator of a common driver, or a proxy for omitted information. Results may change when another variable is added, when the sampling frequency changes, or when different lags are used. There may also be predictive feedback in both directions across dates.

A useful forecasting relationship can therefore coexist with no identified intervention effect. Module 9 teaches what the predictive test says and what it leaves unanswered. This preview is optional and is not part of Module 8’s assessable surface.

8.9 Looking Ahead — Cointegration and Error Correction

Return to the Random Walks

Modules 1–2 showed that two unrelated wandering series can produce an impressive levels regression. Differencing helps us avoid treating unrelated trends as a stable relationship. But must every relationship between nonstationary levels be discarded?

Consider Harry and his dog, Mouse. Both wander; the leash keeps their separation from wandering without bound. Karen walks independently. Knowing Mouse’s location may tell us where to look for Harry even though neither location has a fixed mean.

We can generate that distinction with a shared random-walk component and a stationary separation:

set.seed(637611)
n_preview <- 300
harry <- cumsum(rnorm(n_preview))
karen <- cumsum(rnorm(n_preview))
separation <- as.numeric(arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.6), n = n_preview))
mouse <- harry + separation
wandering <- data.frame(
  t = rep(seq_len(n_preview), 3),
  value = c(harry, mouse, karen),
  series = rep(c("Harry", "Mouse", "Karen"), each = n_preview))
ggplot(wandering, aes(t, value, color = series)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Location", color = NULL,
       title = "Harry and Mouse share a wandering component") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
separation_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(t = seq_len(n_preview), gap = mouse - harry, pair = "Mouse minus Harry"),
  data.frame(t = seq_len(n_preview), gap = karen - harry, pair = "Karen minus Harry"))
ggplot(separation_plot, aes(t, gap)) + geom_line(color = "#315375") +
  facet_wrap(~ pair, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Separation", title = "A shared trend can cancel in a difference")

Here Harry and Mouse are each I(1)I(1), but mouse - harry is I(0)I(0) by construction. Karen minus Harry is a random walk. Real data do not come with that construction label; a convincing picture alone is insufficient evidence.

For two I(1)I(1) series, cointegration means that a nontrivial linear combination is stationary. In the simple normalization,

yt∼I(1),xt∼I(1),yt−a−bxt∼I(0).y_t\sim I(1),\quad x_t\sim I(1),\quad y_t-a-bx_t\sim I(0).

The stationary combination describes a long-run relation, with deviations around it. It does not mean the series are identical, never separate, or are necessarily linked by an identified causal effect.

The Familiar ARDL Contains an Error-Correction Form

Subtract yt−1y_{t-1} from both sides of the ARDL(1,1)(1,1) and use xt=xt−1+Δxtx_t=x_{t-1}+\Delta x_t:

Δyt=α+(ϕ1−1)yt−1+(β0+β1)xt−1+β0Δxt+ϵt. \Delta y_t =\alpha+(\phi_1-1)y_{t-1} +(\beta_0+\beta_1)x_{t-1}+\beta_0\Delta x_t+\epsilon_t.

If ϕ1≠1\phi_1\ne1, the same equation can be written

Δyt=−(1−ϕ1)[yt−1−α1−ϕ1−β0+β11−ϕ1xt−1]+β0Δxt+ϵt. \Delta y_t =-(1-\phi_1) \left[y_{t-1}-\frac{\alpha}{1-\phi_1} -\frac{\beta_0+\beta_1}{1-\phi_1}x_{t-1}\right] +\beta_0\Delta x_t+\epsilon_t.

The last regression term describes short-run change. The bracket is the lagged deviation from a level relation. With ϕ1<1\phi_1<1, a positive deviation contributes negatively to next period’s change, other inputs held fixed. The familiar long-run multiplier reappears inside that relation.

This is algebra, not a cointegration test. The rewriting is available for stationary variables too, and it does not establish that the bracket is stationary for an arbitrary pair of I(1)I(1) series. Cointegration, dynamic adjustment, and admissible conditioning assumptions need their own evidence.

Module 10 develops Engle–Granger testing and error-correction modeling. In particular, a unit-root test applied to estimated cointegrating residuals does not use ordinary ADF critical values without adjustment. We leave the testing workflow, Johansen methods, and ARDL bounds testing outside this introduction. The lesson here is why differencing can remove spurious associations while also throwing away a genuine long-run restriction.

8.10 Looking Ahead — From a Conditional Equation to a System

The ARDL has treated xx as information supplied to the outcome equation. For a long-horizon forecast, or when feedback matters, we may need to model xx as well. A simple reduced-form VAR gives each variable an equation involving both histories:

yt=ay+byyyt−1+byxxt−1+ϵy,t,xt=ax+bxyyt−1+bxxxt−1+ϵx,t. \begin{aligned} y_t&=a_y+b_{yy}y_{t-1}+b_{yx}x_{t-1}+\epsilon_{y,t},\\ x_t&=a_x+b_{xy}y_{t-1}+b_{xx}x_{t-1}+\epsilon_{x,t}. \end{aligned}

The aa and bb subscripts distinguish the two equations in this preview. Each equation has own-lag and cross-lag arrows; these arrows point forward in time. Current reduced-form innovations may be correlated. That correlation is not drawn as two opposing same-period causal arrows and called a DAG.

A VAR models the variables’ joint evolution and can propagate a forecast through both equations. It does not automatically identify causal shocks or turn a correlation into a policy experiment. Modules 11–12 separate the mechanics of a system from the assumptions needed to interpret its shocks.

ARDL is useful precisely because one equation makes these issues visible. It can be a defensible conditional model for a particular question even when other questions call for a system.

Common Pitfalls and Misconceptions

  1. “An ARDL is an ARMA with an extra column.” Our basic ARDL has outcome lags and observed predictor lags, with no explicit MA innovation terms. Regression with ARMA disturbances is related but may impose different restrictions.
  2. “The diagram has an arrow, so the effect is causal.” The arrow records a posited model relationship. Identification requires evidence and assumptions beyond drawing or estimating it.
  3. “An exogenous regressor must be uncorrelated with yy.” The relevant restriction concerns the regressor’s relation to the disturbance after conditioning on the modeled information.
  4. “White-noise errors guarantee exogeneity.” A serially independent structural disturbance can be correlated with a current predictor shock.
  5. “Any feedback invalidates the outcome equation.” Lagged feedback can coexist with a valid sequential conditional mean. Common current shocks or simultaneous determination pose a different problem.
  6. “Lagging xx solves endogeneity.” Persistent omitted information or serially dependent disturbances can still invalidate moments involving lagged regressors.
  7. “A clean residual ACF or robust standard errors establish causality.” Neither does. Diagnostics and standard errors have narrower tasks.
  8. “β1\beta_1 is the entire next-period response.” The response also inherits the current change through the AR terms.
  9. “The cumulative multiplier is just the sum of the β\beta coefficients.” That omits autoregressive propagation. Sum the horizon-specific pulse responses.
  10. “A nonzero long-run denominator is enough.” The response must converge. Check stability before interpreting the ratio as an eventual response.
  11. “A future observed value is allowed because I did not use its outcome.” Future predictor information can leak too. Establish the issue date and release dates.
  12. “Adding information must improve holdout performance.” Extra coefficients bring estimation error, and predictive relationships can change. A simple benchmark can win.

Connection to Enders and Other Texts

Enders, Applied Econometric Time Series, 4th edition, Chapter 5 §2, pp. 267–276, develops ADLs and transfer functions. It is the main companion for conditional dynamic responses. Chapter 5 §4, pp. 281–284, provides context for the difficulties of estimating and interpreting structural multivariate relationships. Chapter 5 §8 and Chapter 6 §§1–3 connect to the later Granger-causality and cointegration modules.

Hamilton, Time Series Analysis, §8.2, pp. 215–219, is a more formal reference for dynamic regression and its inferential qualifications. §11.2, pp. 302–309, develops Granger causality and its predictive interpretation. These are optional depth, not a request to memorize asymptotic arguments.

Hyndman, the 2014 Forecasting: Principles and Practice short-course handout, Chapter 10, especially pp. 109 and 113–114, connects regression to forecasting and lagged predictors. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos’s textbook discussion of regression forecasting also emphasizes the need for future predictor values and the distinction between scenario and ex-ante forecasts.

Textbook convention Course convention and reading advice
ADL versus ARDL Alternative names; check the maximum-lag convention and whether current xx is included.
aja_j for AR coefficients in Enders We use ϕj\phi_j; βℓ\beta_\ell labels predictor coefficients.
Characteristic roots inside the unit circle We state lag-polynomial roots outside. They are reciprocal descriptions of the same stability condition.
Forecasts often carry hats From Module 7 onward we use ỹt+h∣t\tilde y_{t+h\mid t}; hats remain for estimates and fitted values.
Different uses of “multiplier” Specify pulse, cumulative pulse, permanent step, or an innovation-induced input path.
Adjustment coefficient often called α\alpha in ECM/VECM texts In this module α\alpha remains the intercept; we write the adjustment coefficient explicitly as ϕ1−1\phi_1-1.

Practice Problems

Core Practice

  1. Draw a time-unrolled ARDL(1,2)(1,2) diagram, including current and two lagged values of xx, the first lag of yy, and the current outcome disturbance. Identify which arrows disappear when β0=0\beta_0=0. Explain why none of these arrows is itself evidence of causal identification.
  2. For yt=0.3+0.5yt−1+0.6xt−0.1xt−1+ϵty_t=0.3+0.5y_{t-1}+0.6x_t-0.1x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t, calculate the conditional mean when yt−1=2y_{t-1}=2, xt=1x_t=1, and xt−1=3x_{t-1}=3, under the stated zero-conditional-mean assumption. Distinguish this mean from a realization, an estimated fitted value, and a forecast.
  3. Explain how ϵt\epsilon_t could be white noise but correlated with xtx_t. Use an economic example and say what a residual ACF can and cannot diagnose.
  4. Re-run the three-case simulation with 200 and 2,000 observations per sample. Compare average coefficient estimates and their dispersion. Explain which discrepancy more observations can reduce and which they cannot repair.
  5. For ϕ1=0.5\phi_1=0.5, β0=0.6\beta_0=0.6, and β1=−0.1\beta_1=-0.1, compute pulse responses at horizons 0–3, cumulative responses through those horizons, and the stable long-run step multiplier. Explain each in words.
  6. In the previous problem, suppose a unit shock to xx produces the path 1,0.8,0.82,…1,0.8,0.8^2,\ldots. Calculate the outcome response through horizon two and explain why it differs from an imposed one-period pulse.
  7. Compare the lag-selection code using a common sample with a version that lets each model omit only its own missing lags. Explain why differences in their IC rankings would be difficult to interpret.
  8. A model uses current monthly claims to predict current monthly unemployment. Describe the release information needed to call its fitted prediction a nowcast. Identify a design that would instead leak future information.
  9. In the empirical exercise, choose an alternative lag order using training data only and report its 2018–2019 RMSE and MAE beside the supplied benchmarks. Retain the same forecast origins and dates. Describe the comparison without claiming a universal model ranking or causal effect.
  10. A colleague reports a long-run multiplier of −12-12 from ϕ̂1=1.05\hat\phi_1=1.05 and β̂0+β̂1=0.6\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1=0.6. Use a response path to explain the problem. Separately explain why a near-one but stable estimate still warrants care about uncertainty.

Beyond Core (optional)

  • Derive the conditional regression coefficients in the shared-shock simulation for a general shock correlation rr and predictor persistence ρx\rho_x.
  • Extend ardl_multipliers()’s examples to two outcome lags and explain the response shape using the general recursion.
  • In the Harry–Mouse simulation, replace the stationary separation with another independent random walk. Explain which defining property of cointegration disappears.
  • Write both directions of a lag-only predictive model and list the restrictions that would be examined in a bilateral Granger-causality exercise. Testing is developed in Module 9.

Key Takeaways

  1. ARDL adds observed information to a dynamic outcome equation. Current and lagged predictors are different from the innovation lags of an MA model.
  2. Exogeneity is about the disturbance and the conditioning information. A sequential conditional-mean restriction can allow lagged feedback while excluding correlation with current predictor innovations.
  3. Prediction, conditional response, and causal response are different claims. A regression can forecast well and have clean residuals while failing to recover structural DGP coefficients.
  4. Dynamic responses follow every route through the equation. The next-period pulse response includes both the direct lag coefficient and inherited outcome persistence. A stable long-run multiplier sums that propagation.
  5. A forecast needs an honest calendar. Future predictors, reporting delays, aggregation, and revisions matter alongside model coefficients.
  6. The familiar workflow still applies. Use sensible transformations, compare lag specifications on a common sample, diagnose residuals, and evaluate forecasts against simple benchmarks.

Looking Ahead — The Next Questions

Module 9 asks whether the history of one variable adds predictive information beyond the history already being used: Granger causality. It retains the stationary baseline and makes the information set explicit. Module 10 returns to nonstationary levels and asks when a stable relationship survives between them: cointegration and error correction.

The later VAR modules then model the joint evolution of the variables. The thread connecting these topics is already on the opening diagram: which information enters, when does it enter, and what interpretation do the assumptions justify?
